documents.unit: Office of the Provost, Generative AI in Teaching and Learning
documents.title: Guidance for Faculty & Students
documents.stance_why: The FAQs set no default rule. They say instructors must make explicit "which uses of Gen-AI are permitted in coursework, if any, and which are prohibited", and tell students that "Some instructors may permit or even encourage some uses". So the decision is delegated to instructors, and the stance is delegates.
documents.summary: Provost and Center for Teaching Excellence FAQs for faculty and students on Gen-AI in teaching and learning. They leave AI rules to instructors, require that syllabi state them, and add advice on discussion, assignment design, privacy, disclosure, grading and detectors.

units.why: The opening says "These FAQs provide guidance about the appropriate uses of these tools in teaching and learning at the University." It sets purpose and scope for the whole page, so P56, not a rule type.
units.anchor: These FAQs provide guidance about the appropriate uses of these tools in teaching and learning
units.policy: The FAQs give guidance about the appropriate uses of generative AI tools in teaching and learning at the University.

units.why: The page says its own advice is provisional: "This guidance may be revised as additional benefits and risks of this technology emerge". That is a statement about revising the policy, so P54.
units.anchor: This guidance may be revised as additional benefits and risks of this technology emerge
units.policy: The Provost's guidance may be revised as benefits and risks emerge, as the technology develops, or as new kinds of Gen-AI tools become available.
units.resolution_why: A: actor=admin; B: actor=all. Both coders coded the sentence P54 and differed only on actor (A admin, B all). The sentence is the Provost's office saying its own guidance may be revised, so the body that revises it is the Provost's office (admin). Final: actor=admin.

units.why: The FAQ advises "A frank, open discussion with your class will help to shape your students' perspectives". It tells instructors to talk with students about AI rather than only state a rule, which is P66.
units.anchor: A frank, open discussion with your class will help to shape your students’ perspectives
units.policy: Instructors should hold a frank, open discussion with the class about generative AI to shape students' perspectives and approach to coursework.
units.resolution_why: A: unit_stance=neutral; B: unit_stance=encourage. Both coded P66, instructor, course-start, should; they differed on unit_stance (A neutral, B encourage). The sentence advises holding a class discussion about the rules; it takes no position on whether students should use AI, so neutral. Final: unit_stance=neutral.

units.why: The faculty FAQ says "You might begin the conversation by asking your students for their perspectives on this technology and what role(s) it should (or should not) play". It is a suggestion about discussing the rules with students, so P66; P67 (co-create the policy) is not stated, since nothing says the policy is made with students.
units.anchor: asking your students for their perspectives on this technology and what role(s) it should (or
units.policy: Instructors might begin the conversation with students by asking for their perspectives on the technology and what role(s) it should or should not play in a class like theirs.
units.resolution_why: Only B coded it. The sentence is a real suggestion to instructors, but B's P67 (co-create) goes beyond the text, which says only to start a conversation and ask for perspectives. Coded P66, may, neutral.

units.why: "Talk about the learning objectives for each assignment" is advice to explain the reason behind allowing, limiting or prohibiting AI. P66 fits better than P83 because the point is explaining to students, not deriving the rule from objectives.
units.anchor: Talk about the learning objectives for each assignment.
units.fit_note: Also says the objectives clarify the rationale for allowing, limiting or prohibiting AI (P83 flavor). Also says the talk helps students see what they would miss by not doing the work (explaining the rules to students, P66).
units.resolution_why: A: policy_type=P66; B: policy_type=P83. Both coders agree this advice is to instructors and both quote the same sentence; A coded P66 (explain the rules and rationale to students), B coded P83 (align AI decisions with learning objectives). The passage says talking about learning objectives 'will clarify your rationale for allowing, limiting, or prohibiting the use of AI tools', i.e. it is a way of explaining the rules to students, so P66; P83 is noted in the fit_note. Final: policy_type=P66.

units.why: "Point out – or better, demonstrate – these tools' limitations" asks instructors to show students that AI output may be false or biased. It is about verification, so P31, addressed to instructors.
units.anchor: Point out – or better, demonstrate – these tools’ limitations.
units.fit_note: Addressed to instructors to show students the limits, not to students to verify. Addressed to instructors as a teaching move (demonstrate limits) rather than to students as a verification duty.

units.why: "Acknowledge that these tools can be used to aid learning, and encourage your students to use them in appropriate ways." It tells instructors to encourage appropriate AI use. No exact type matches (P02 is a default stance), so nearest is P02.
units.anchor: encourage your students to use them in appropriate ways
units.policy: Instructors should acknowledge that these tools can aid learning and encourage students to use them in appropriate ways.
units.fit_note: Instructor advice to encourage appropriate use and frame restrictions as thoughtful, not a set default stance.
units.resolution_why: A: policy_type=P02; B: policy_type=P66. A coded P02 (encourage appropriate use), B coded P66 (explain rules). The sentence tells instructors to 'acknowledge that these tools can be used to aid learning, and encourage your students to use them in appropriate ways'; the act is encouragement of AI use, so P02, with a fit_note that it is advice about framing, not a default stance. Final: policy_type=P02.

units.why: Lists example recommended uses, "answering simple factual questions, breaking down complex concepts"; tutor-like understanding (P12).
units.anchor: answering simple factual questions, breaking down complex concepts
units.resolution_why: A: phase=during-work, unit_stance=permit; B: phase=course-start, unit_stance=encourage. Coders differed on phase (A during-work, B course-start) and unit_stance (A permit, B encourage). The sentence tells instructors what to recommend ('Your recommendations ... may include'), so the act is communicating to students: course-start; it lists uses that are allowed ('may include'), so permit. Final: phase=course-start, unit_stance=permit.

units.why: The same sentence recommends "checking paper drafts for grammar and readability"; a writing-support permission (P91), separate from the tutor use.
units.anchor: checking paper drafts for grammar and readability
units.resolution_why: A: phase=during-work; B: phase=course-start. Both permit editing support (P91, may); they differed on phase (A during-work, B course-start). Same instructor-recommendation passage as the previous unit ('Your recommendations ... may include ... checking paper drafts'), so course-start, for consistency. Final: phase=course-start.

units.why: The same sentence suggests serving as a "Socratic opponent" that raises objections to an argument. It is feedback on the student's own thinking, nearest P14 (self-checks of knowledge), though P15 (exploring approaches) is also close.
units.anchor: serving as a “Socratic opponent” that raises objections to a submitted piece of argumentation
units.policy: Recommended uses of Gen-AI may include serving as a "Socratic opponent" that raises objections to a submitted piece of argumentation.
units.fit_note: Critique of the student's own argument, rather than practice problems or study guides. AI as a critic of one's argument rather than idea generation.
units.resolution_why: A: policy_type=P14, phase=during-work; B: policy_type=P15, phase=course-start. Coders differed on type (A P14, B P15) and phase. The 'Socratic opponent' raises objections to a submitted argument, i.e. review and feedback on work rather than idea generation, so P14 (practice, study aids, review). Phase course-start as in the sibling recommendation units. Final: policy_type=P14, phase=course-start.

units.why: "Students should always critically assess the responses generated by the tools and check factual claims against reliable sources." Students are told to verify output, which is P31.
units.anchor: Students should always critically assess the responses generated by the tools
units.policy: Students should always critically assess the responses generated by the tools and check factual claims against reliable sources.

units.why: "Consider requiring them to comprehensively explain how they used AI tools as part of the assignment" is advice that instructors ask for disclosure. P24 fits; the actor is the instructor.
units.anchor: Consider requiring them to comprehensively explain how they used AI tools as part of the
units.policy: Instructors should consider requiring students to comprehensively explain how they used AI tools as part of the assignment.
units.resolution_why: A: policy_type=P24; B: policy_type=P26. A coded P24 (disclose AI use), B coded P26 (reflections). The passage: 'Consider requiring them to comprehensively explain how they used AI tools'; it points to the acknowledgment FAQ and asks for an explanation of use attached to the assignment, i.e. disclosure, so P24; P26 requires keeping transcripts, logs or reflections, which the passage does not name. Final: policy_type=P24.

units.why: "Remind your students that they are ultimately responsible for the work they submit." Students own what they submit, so P29, with the instructor as actor.
units.anchor: Remind your students that they are ultimately responsible for the work they submit.

units.why: The FAQ says cheating "will deprive them of the opportunity to develop knowledge and skills that will serve them throughout their lives and careers". The reason given is lost skill-building, so P41.
units.anchor: It will deprive them of the opportunity to develop knowledge and skills
units.policy: Cheating, including inappropriate use of AI tools, will deprive students of the opportunity to develop knowledge and skills that will serve them throughout their lives and careers.

units.why: The analogy "cheating is like going to the gym and allowing someone else to do your workout for you" illustrates why outsourcing practice defeats the purpose, so P41 again.
units.anchor: cheating is like going to the gym and allowing someone else to do your workout

units.why: The sentence "Many involve shifting the focus from product to process, which has been shown to be beneficial for learning" recommends process-focused design, so P35.
units.anchor: shifting the focus from product to process, which has been shown to be beneficial for
units.policy: Many strategies to deter inappropriate Gen-AI use involve shifting the focus from product to process, which has been shown to be beneficial for learning.
units.resolution_why: Only A coded it. The sentence 'Many [strategies] involve shifting the focus from product to process, which has been shown to be beneficial for learning' is a real statement of the rationale for assignment redesign; kept as P35 informs.

units.why: "Instead of a few high-stakes assignments, have students complete several lower-stakes assignments" restructures assessment to deter AI misuse, so P35.
units.anchor: Instead of a few high-stakes assignments, have students complete several lower-stakes assignments.

units.why: "Break large projects into multiple assignments" is an assignment redesign suggestion to deter AI misuse, so P35.
units.anchor: Break large projects into multiple assignments
units.policy: Instructors should break large projects into multiple assignments, such as idea development, initial research, preliminary drafts, and a final paper or project.

units.why: "Ask students to include reflections on their methods at each stage" requires written reflections on process, which fits P26 (reflections).
units.anchor: Ask students to include reflections on their methods at each stage
units.policy: Instructors should ask students to include reflections on their methods at each stage and to explain how revisions respond to feedback.
units.fit_note: Reflection on the work process generally, not specifically on AI use.
units.resolution_why: Only A coded it. 'Ask students to include reflections on their methods at each stage' is a separate assignment-design suggestion in the same bullet as the multi-assignment unit; kept (P26 with the fit_note that the reflection is on process, not AI use).

units.why: "Design writing prompts around examples not found in Gen-AI data" is an assignment redesign to make AI less useful, so P35.
units.anchor: Design writing prompts around examples not found in Gen-AI data
units.policy: Instructors should design writing prompts around examples not found in Gen-AI data, such as fictional scenarios developed in class, recent local events, or material from guest speakers or other students.

units.why: "Ask students to present their work, individually or in small groups, discussing their methods" checks understanding through presentations and questions, which is P34.
units.anchor: Ask students to present their work, individually or in small groups, discussing their methods
units.policy: Instructors should ask students to present their work, individually or in small groups, discussing their methods at each stage and answering questions.

units.why: "You can take Teaching in a World with Generative AI, a course created by UVA faculty and staff" offers instructors training before setting policy, which is P63.
units.anchor: a course created by UVA faculty and staff to enable UVA instructors
units.policy: UVA instructors can take the course Teaching in a World with Generative AI to make informed decisions about whether and how to incorporate Gen-AI into their teaching.

units.why: "The Center regularly hosts talks and offers workshops on Gen-AI" is faculty support, P63.
units.anchor: The Center regularly hosts talks and offers workshops on Gen-AI.
units.resolution_why: A: phase=general; B: phase=before-course. Both P63 informs; they differed on phase (A general, B before-course). The sentence is a statement of fact about CTE events ('regularly hosts talks and offers workshops'), not a step in setting up a course, so general. Final: phase=general.

units.why: "these engines may save your entire conversation, including every prompt you enter, to be used in training the system" warns about data retention and training use, which is P50.
units.anchor: these engines may save your entire conversation, including every prompt you enter
units.policy: Many Gen-AI engines, including ChatGPT, may save the user's account information and entire conversation, including every prompt, to be used in training the system.

units.why: "UVA Copilot Chat... includes contractual data protection of university information" points to a vetted tool whose prompts stay in a UVA tenant. Preferring vetted tools is P50; P92 (use licensed tools) is weaker because no duty to use it is stated here.
units.anchor: UVA Copilot Chat, which is UVA’s licensed version of Microsoft’s Copilot, includes contractual data protection
units.policy: UVA Copilot Chat, UVA's licensed version of Microsoft's Copilot, includes contractual data protection of university information; prompt data stays in a UVA-specific tenant and is not used for training.
units.resolution_why: A: policy_type=P50, actor=all; B: policy_type=P92, actor=instructor. A coded P50 (all), B coded P92 (instructor). The sentence states that UVA Copilot Chat 'includes contractual data protection'; it states a fact about a vetted tool and does not tell anyone to use it, so P50 (prefer vetted tools / protect data) not P92. It sits in the faculty FAQ on privacy, so the actor is instructor. Final: policy_type=P50, actor=instructor.

units.why: "ITS has provided helpful guidelines for the Responsible Use of Generative AI Tools at UVA." Points to other guidance, P115.
units.anchor: ITS has provided helpful guidelines for the Responsible Use of Generative AI Tools at UVA.

units.why: "May I incorporate Gen-AI into my teaching? Yes." Instructors are told they may use AI in their teaching, an allow-by-default answer, so P02 with the instructor as actor.
units.anchor: Incorporating this technology into your teaching can be useful
units.policy: Instructors may incorporate Gen-AI into their teaching; doing so can be useful because many students are experimenting with these tools.
units.fit_note: Permission for instructors to incorporate AI into teaching, not a default student rule.
units.resolution_why: A: unit_stance=permit; B: unit_stance=encourage. Both P02; they differed on modality (A may/permit, B may/encourage on unit_stance). The FAQ answers 'May I incorporate Gen-AI into my teaching? Yes. Incorporating this technology into your teaching can be useful', which grants permission, so permit. Final: unit_stance=permit.

units.why: "It is important that they learn how to use them appropriately and that they understand these tools' limitations" gives learning to use AI well as a reason for teaching it. P44.
units.anchor: It is important that they learn how to use them appropriately
units.policy: It is important that students learn how to use Gen-AI tools appropriately and understand their limitations and the ethical issues connected with their use.
units.resolution_why: A: actor=all, phase=general; B: actor=instructor, phase=before-course. Both P44; they differed on actor (A all, B instructor) and phase (A general, B before-course). The sentence is in the faculty FAQ and justifies teaching students to use AI appropriately; it is a principle (general) addressed to instructors. Final: actor=instructor, phase=general.

units.why: "we strongly recommend that you ask them to use UVA Copilot Chat" points instructors to the university-licensed tool for assignments that use AI. P17 is the nearest (sanctioned tool); it is a strong recommendation, not a requirement.
units.anchor: we strongly recommend that you ask them to use UVA Copilot Chat
units.policy: If instructors want students to use Gen-AI tools in an assignment, they are strongly recommended to ask them to use UVA Copilot Chat.
units.fit_note: University-wide licensed tool recommended for assignments, not a course-specific tool.

units.why: "Students should not be required to create accounts" for unlicensed tools because they collect phone numbers or personal data; an access rule (P51) with a privacy motive.
units.anchor: students should not be required to create accounts for these tools
units.fit_note: Reason given is personal-information privacy rather than cost. Limits what instructors can require, to protect students' personal data.
units.resolution_why: A: policy_type=P50; B: policy_type=P51. A coded P50 (data protection), B coded P51 (do not require tools), and B also coded the same sentence a second time as an informing unit (dropped as a duplicate). The rule itself is 'students should not be required to create accounts for these tools'; P51 covers 'AI is optional or not required', and the privacy motive goes in the fit_note. Coded should-not / restrict as in both. Final: policy_type=P51.

units.why: Notes students may worry about uploading original work since it "will add the work to the tool’s data set"; a privacy and IP fact (P50 chosen because the concern is data entering the tool).
units.anchor: Students may have privacy or intellectual property concerns about uploading their original work to a
units.policy: Students may have privacy or intellectual property concerns about uploading their original work to a Gen-AI tool, since this adds the work to the tool's data set.
units.resolution_why: A: policy_type=P52; B: policy_type=P50. A coded P52 (licensing and copyright), B coded P50 (data protection). The passage is about privacy and the work entering the tool's data set, so P50; A's policy wording is kept because the anchor is cut off. Final: policy_type=P50.

units.why: "You must provide alternative ways to complete the assignment" when students must upload original work; an alternatives rule (P51).
units.anchor: you must provide alternative ways to complete the assignment
units.fit_note: Alternative is required for privacy and IP reasons, not cost.
units.resolution_why: A: unit_stance=require; B: unit_stance=restrict. Both P51 with must; they differed on unit_stance (A require, B restrict). The rule 'you must provide alternative ways to complete the assignment' limits assignments that force students to upload work; it does not require AI use, so restrict. Final: unit_stance=restrict.

units.why: "It is important for instructors to make explicit in their syllabi and assignment descriptions which uses of Gen-AI are permitted" states the syllabus-statement expectation. P09.
units.anchor: make explicit in their syllabi and assignment descriptions which uses of Gen-AI are permitted
units.policy: Instructors should make explicit in their syllabi and assignment descriptions which uses of Gen-AI are permitted in coursework, if any, and which are prohibited.
units.resolution_why: A: phase=course-start; B: phase=before-course. Both P09; phase differed (A course-start, B before-course). Making uses explicit 'in their syllabi and assignment descriptions' is communicating expectations, so course-start. Final: phase=course-start.

units.why: "Using Gen-AI for completing coursework in ways that are prohibited by the course instructor may be a violation of the Honor Code" ties instructor rules to integrity enforcement, P36.
units.anchor: ways that are prohibited by the course instructor may be a violation of the Honor
units.policy: Using Gen-AI for coursework in ways prohibited by the course instructor may be a violation of the Honor Code.
units.resolution_why: A: actor=student; B: actor=instructor. Both P36; they differed on actor (A student, B instructor). The sentence says that using AI in prohibited ways 'may be a violation of the Honor Code'; the consequence binds students, though it sits in the faculty FAQ. Student. Final: actor=student.

units.why: "The Center for Teaching Excellence has compiled resources... including an interactive syllabus statement drafting tool." Provides syllabus drafting help, P110.
units.anchor: including an interactive syllabus statement drafting tool
units.policy: The Center for Teaching Excellence provides resources for talking with students about Gen-AI, including an interactive syllabus statement drafting tool.

units.why: "explain concepts at different levels of complexity" describes AI as a tutor for understanding without direct help on assignments, which is P12.
units.anchor: these tools can explain concepts at different levels of complexity
units.policy: Gen-AI tools can explain concepts at different levels of complexity, contributing to learning without providing direct assistance on assignments.
units.resolution_why: A: actor=student, phase=during-work; B: actor=instructor, phase=course-start. Both P12 may permit; they differed on actor (A student, B instructor) and phase (A during-work, B course-start). The sentence says what the tools can do for students' learning ('these tools can explain concepts at different levels'); it is about students' own study use, so student / during-work. Final: actor=student, phase=during-work.

units.why: "create virtual flash cards and other study aids" is a study-aid use, P14.
units.anchor: Students can also use the tools to create virtual flash cards and other study aids.

units.why: "You may wish to share these uses with your students and to ask them to describe other ways that they are using Gen-AI as a study aid." Instructors are invited to open a conversation about study uses, P66.
units.anchor: You may wish to share these uses with your students
units.policy: Instructors may share study uses of Gen-AI with students and ask them to describe other ways they use Gen-AI as a study aid.
units.resolution_why: A: unit_stance=neutral; B: unit_stance=encourage. Both P66; they differed on unit_stance (A neutral, B encourage). 'You may wish to share these uses with your students' tells instructors to communicate permitted study uses; it takes no position itself, so neutral. Final: unit_stance=neutral.

units.why: "You should also caution them that responses should always be independently assessed and checked against reliable sources such as the course textbook." Verification advice to instructors, P31.
units.anchor: responses should always be independently assessed and checked against reliable sources
units.policy: Instructors should caution students that Gen-AI responses should always be independently assessed and checked against reliable sources such as the course textbook.

units.why: Instructors "may not enter a student's original work into any AI tool that will add that work to the tool’s data set"; a faculty data-protection rule with no exact type, nearest P50.
units.anchor: instructors may not enter a student's original work into any AI tool that will add
units.fit_note: A forbids instructors from putting a student's original work into an AI tool that adds it to the tool's data set, because the work is in most cases the student's intellectual property. This is a data-protection rule on instructors grounded in student IP, not on students' own data (A coded UNCOVERED with that note; kept here as a partial fit).
units.resolution_why: A: policy_type=UNCOVERED; B: policy_type=P50. A coded UNCOVERED, B coded P50 with a fit_note. The rule bars instructors from entering a student's original work into a tool that keeps it in its data set; it is a data-protection rule (P50 covers 'AI tools store prompts' and protecting confidential data), so assign P50 with a fit_note rather than UNCOVERED. Final: policy_type=P50.

units.why: "AI tools are not effective for grading most kinds of assignments" is a faculty-use caution about AI grading; P101 (AI grading conditions) is nearer than P46, which says only humans grade.
units.anchor: AI tools are not effective for grading most kinds of assignments, including writing assignments.
units.fit_note: A statement of ineffectiveness rather than a condition. Says AI is ineffective for grading; states no conditions for use.
units.resolution_why: A: unit_stance=restrict; B: unit_stance=neutral. Both P101 informs; unit_stance differed (A restrict, B neutral). 'AI tools are not effective for grading most kinds of assignments' is a statement of fact; the position on grading is taken in the separate discouragement unit, so neutral. Final: unit_stance=neutral.

units.why: "some AI tools can help to ease the grading process, for example by organizing the work and facilitating the use of rubrics" permits limited AI help with grading. P101.
units.anchor: some AI tools can help to ease the grading process, for example by organizing the
units.policy: Some AI tools can help to ease the grading process, for example by organizing the work and facilitating the use of rubrics.
units.fit_note: A permissive suggestion to use university-provided grading tools, not a condition.
units.resolution_why: A: modality=informs; B: modality=may. Both P101, permit; modality differed (A informs, B may). 'Some AI tools can help to ease the grading process' states a fact about capability and grants no instruction, so informs; unit_stance permit. Final: modality=informs.

units.why: "Faculty... are encouraged to explore Gradescope, iRubric, and other tools provided by the University" points instructors to university-provided tools. P92 is the nearest; the named tools are not necessarily generative AI.
units.anchor: encouraged to explore Gradescope, iRubric, and other tools provided by the University
units.policy: Faculty wishing to make grading more efficient and consistent are encouraged to explore Gradescope, iRubric, and other tools provided by the University.
units.fit_note: Grading tools provided by the University; the page does not say they are generative AI.
units.resolution_why: Only A coded it. 'Faculty ... are encouraged to explore Gradescope, iRubric, and other tools provided by the University' is a real recommendation of university-provided grading tools; kept (P92, should, encourage).

units.why: "The University discourages instructors from using Gen-AI detectors for the purpose of detecting academic fraud" states that detectors should not be relied on, P39.
units.anchor: The University discourages instructors from using Gen-AI detectors
units.policy: The University discourages instructors from using Gen-AI detectors for the purpose of detecting academic fraud.

units.why: The task force report is quoted: "these [detecting] tools are notoriously unreliable and hence using them is usually counterproductive and can be risky." Reason for not relying on detectors, P39.
units.anchor: these [detecting] tools are notoriously unreliable
units.policy: Gen-AI detecting tools are notoriously unreliable and hence using them is usually counterproductive and can be risky (task force report, p. 6).

units.why: Instructors "may not upload a student’s original work to those detectors" because detectors keep content; data and IP protection of student work (P50).
units.anchor: instructors may not upload a student’s original work to those detectors
units.fit_note: A forbids instructors from uploading a student's original work to AI detectors, because most detectors add submitted content to their databases and the work is in most cases the student's intellectual property. A coded UNCOVERED; kept here as a partial fit to a data-protection type.
units.resolution_why: A: policy_type=UNCOVERED; B: policy_type=P50. A coded UNCOVERED, B coded P50 with a fit_note. Same data-set rule as the grading passage, applied to detectors, so the same type (P50 with fit_note). Final: policy_type=P50.

units.why: "Guides for students on how to \"trick\" AI content detectors are widely available" says detection can be evaded, a limit on control. P82.
units.anchor: Guides for students on how to “trick” AI content detectors are widely available.
units.resolution_why: Only A coded it. 'Guides for students on how to "trick" AI content detectors are widely available' is a fact the FAQ uses to explain why detection is weak; kept as P82 informs.

units.why: "You should not enter sensitive, personal, or proprietary information into any Gen-AI system." Data protection for students, P50.
units.anchor: You should not enter sensitive, personal, or proprietary information into any Gen-AI system.

units.why: "Some instructors may permit or even encourage some uses of Gen-AI in your coursework." Tells students the rule varies by instructor, P04.
units.anchor: Some instructors may permit or even encourage some uses of Gen-AI in your coursework.

units.why: "When in doubt about whether a particular way of using these tools is permissible, talk with your instructor." Directly P10.
units.anchor: When in doubt about whether a particular way of using these tools is permissible, talk
units.resolution_why: A: phase=during-work; B: phase=course-start. Both P10; phase differed (A during-work, B course-start). 'When in doubt about whether a particular way of using these tools is permissible, talk with your instructor' applies at the moment of using AI on coursework, so during-work. Final: phase=during-work.

units.why: "you should clearly indicate the tool used, how you used it, the prompts you used" names the tool, how used and the prompts. P25 (details of the citation), including for permitted use.
units.anchor: you should clearly indicate the tool used, how you used it, the prompts you used
units.policy: If you have used AI in an assignment, even in ways explicitly permitted by the instructor, you should clearly indicate the tool used, how you used it, the prompts you used, and when appropriate your efforts to fact-check the results.

units.why: "Presenting work produced by Gen-AI as one's own" may violate the Honor Code. This is a separate rule from instructor-prohibited use in the same sentence; P36.
units.anchor: Presenting work produced by Gen-AI as one’s own
units.policy: Presenting work produced by Gen-AI as one's own may be a violation of the Honor Code.
units.fit_note: Framed as an Honor Code violation (P36) rather than a flat ban.
units.resolution_why: A: policy_type=P36, modality=informs, unit_stance=restrict; B: policy_type=P19, modality=must-not, unit_stance=prohibit. A coded P36 (restrict), B coded P19 (prohibit) for 'Presenting work produced by Gen-AI as one's own'. The sentence says this 'may be [a violation] of the Honor Code', a misconduct classification, so P36; the act is passing off AI work, so unit_stance prohibit. Final: policy_type=P36, modality=informs, unit_stance=prohibit.

units.why: "Using Gen-AI for coursework in ways not permitted by the course instructor may be violations of the Honor Code" is the student-addressed misconduct rule (P36).
units.anchor: using Gen-AI for coursework in ways not permitted by the course instructor may be violations
units.resolution_why: Only B coded it. The student FAQ says 'using Gen-AI for coursework in ways not permitted by the course instructor may be violations of the Honor Code'. A coded the faculty-FAQ version and the 'presenting as one's own' half only, so this student-addressed misconduct rule is kept (P36).

units.why: The MLA quote says "cite a generative AI tool whenever you paraphrase, quote, or incorporate into your own work any content". That is a duty to cite AI-created content, P24.
units.anchor: cite a generative AI tool whenever you paraphrase, quote, or incorporate into your own work

documents.title: Setting Boundaries for AI Use Through Syllabus Statements
documents.stance_why: The page says "UVA instructors are allowed and encouraged to set their own course-level AI policies" and offers examples that differ widely (ban, disclosure, per-assignment rules). It sets no university rule itself, so the stance is delegates. Examples are non-computing courses.
documents.summary: A Center for Teaching Excellence collection of example AI syllabus statements from UVA courses in English, engineering and society, nursing, law and business. It also quotes the Provost guidance that instructors set their own course-level policies. The examples range from a full ban to required disclosure to required use.

units.why: "Students appreciate clear guidance on which uses of generative AI are permitted in coursework, if any, and which are prohibited." It gives the reason for stating boundaries in syllabi, P09.
units.anchor: Students appreciate clear guidance on which uses of generative AI are permitted in coursework
units.policy: Students appreciate clear guidance on which uses of generative AI are permitted in coursework, if any, and which are prohibited.
units.fit_note: A reason students value clear statements rather than a requirement.

units.why: "The syllabus statements in this collection are examples that instructors can use" offers sample statements, P110.
units.anchor: The syllabus statements in this collection are examples that instructors can use
units.policy: The syllabus statements in this collection are examples instructors can use to set and communicate boundaries for student AI use that align with their course goals and teaching values.
units.resolution_why: A: modality=may; B: modality=informs. Both P110; modality differed (A may, B informs). 'The syllabus statements in this collection are examples that instructors can use' says instructors may use them, so may. Final: modality=may.

units.anchor: boundaries for student AI use that align with their course goals and teaching values
units.resolution_why: Only B coded it. The second clause of the intro sentence, 'boundaries for student AI use that align with their course goals and teaching values', is a distinct rule (align AI rules with course goals), so kept (P83).

units.why: "UVA instructors are allowed and encouraged to set their own course-level AI policies." The decision is left to each instructor, which is P04.
units.anchor: UVA instructors are allowed and encouraged to set their own course-level AI policies.

units.anchor: make explicit in their syllabi and assignment descriptions which uses of Gen-AI are permitted
units.policy: Instructors should make explicit in their syllabi and assignment descriptions which uses of Gen-AI are permitted in coursework, if any, and which are prohibited.
units.resolution_why: A: phase=course-start; B: phase=before-course. Both P09; phase differed (A course-start, B before-course). Making uses explicit in syllabi is communicating expectations, so course-start. Final: phase=course-start.

units.why: "may be a violation of the Honor Code" for use that the instructor prohibits. Quoted Provost excerpt, P36.
units.anchor: ways that are prohibited by the course instructor may be a violation of the Honor
units.policy: Using Gen-AI for completing coursework in ways prohibited by the course instructor may be a violation of the Honor Code.

units.why: Bruff notes the example "invites his students into further discussion about learning to write" and gives "a rationale for that boundary that points to his learning goals". The rule is explained to students, P66.
units.anchor: provides a rationale for that boundary that points to his learning goals
units.policy: The example policy gives students a rationale for its boundary that points to the instructor's learning goals and invites students into further discussion about learning to write.

documents.title: AI Policy (student use of AI tools in Data Science courses)
documents.stance_why: The policy requires syllabi to state AI rules but also sets a School default: AI "is permitted with the following activities... at no penalty", some uses are "NOT permitted", and it ends with "the use of foundation models is encouraged". units.why: "Substantially identical" work is "grounds for an investigation of plagiarism, regardless of whether the work was produced by AI"; similarity as the trigger for review (P40).
units.anchor: if a student's work is substantially identical to another student's work, that constitutes grounds for
units.fit_note: Treats identical work as grounds for investigation rather than describing a similarity tool. Concerns identical work across students whatever the source.
units.resolution_why: A: policy_type=P36, unit_stance=restrict; B: policy_type=P40, unit_stance=prohibit. A coded P36 (misconduct), B coded P40 (similarity as evidence). The passage says work substantially identical to another student's 'constitutes grounds for an investigation of plagiarism, regardless of whether the work was produced by AI'. It treats similarity as evidence for an investigation, so P40, with a fit_note that it states grounds for investigation. Coded informs; unit_stance restrict (not prohibit, as the passage sets grounds for investigation). Final: policy_type=P40, unit_stance=restrict.

units.why: Students are responsible for "Clarifying any incomplete, inconsistent, or confusing rules in the syllabus with the instructor before beginning any assignments". Ask before starting, P10.
units.anchor: Clarifying any incomplete, inconsistent, or confusing rules in the syllabus with the instructor
units.policy: Students are responsible for clarifying any incomplete, inconsistent or confusing syllabus rules with the instructor before beginning the assignments in question.

units.why: Instructors are responsible for "Clearly communicating the expectations for, and limits of, AI usage inside and outside of class." Syllabus communication duty, P09.
units.anchor: Clearly communicating the expectations for, and limits of, AI usage inside and outside of class.

units.why: "Providing a statement on how coursework will be assessed" is a required statement for instructors. It fits P09 only partly, because it is about assessment rather than AI rules.
units.anchor: Providing a statement on how coursework will be assessed;
units.fit_note: Requires a statement on how coursework will be assessed, not AI rules directly. The syllabus must state the assessment approach, not specifically an AI use rule.

units.why: "Describing how the use of AI tools will be interpreted with respect to the honor code" requires instructors to say how AI use relates to integrity rules. P36 is nearest.
units.anchor: Describing how the use of AI tools will be interpreted with respect to the honor
units.fit_note: Instructors must describe how AI use relates to the honor code; it does not itself classify misuse. A duty to explain the mapping, not the classification itself.

units.why: "Describing how, when, and in which instances students should disclose the use of AI tools on assignments" requires instructors to set disclosure rules, P24.
units.anchor: Describing how, when, and in which instances students should disclose the use of AI tools
units.policy: Instructors are responsible for describing how, when, and in which instances students should disclose the use of AI tools on assignments.
units.fit_note: Directed at instructors to specify disclosure rules. A duty on instructors to specify disclosure rules.

units.why: "Describing how the use of AI tools will be enforced" matches P123, saying how misuse will be detected and handled.
units.anchor: Describing how the use of AI tools will be enforced.

units.why: Instructors are encouraged to "disclose usage of AI tools in the preparation of their class"; instructor disclosure (P47).
units.anchor: Disclose usage of AI tools in the preparation of their class;
units.resolution_why: A: phase=course-start; B: phase=before-course. Both P47 should; phase differed (A course-start, B before-course). 'Disclose usage of AI tools in the preparation of their class' concerns preparing the course, so before-course. Final: phase=before-course.

units.why: Instructors are encouraged to "Model the behavior they expect to see from their students", i.e. model responsible use. P112.
units.anchor: Model the behavior they expect to see from their students
units.policy: Instructors are encouraged to model the behavior they expect to see from their students.
units.resolution_why: A: phase=during-work; B: phase=before-course. Both P112 should; phase differed (A during-work, B before-course). Modelling behavior happens while teaching the course, so during-work. Final: phase=during-work.

units.why: Instructors are encouraged to "Address the perceived difference between AI constructing answers and using internet resources to learn" in the syllabus. This is explaining the rules to students, P66.
units.anchor: Address the perceived difference between “AI constructing answers” and “using internet resources to learn”
units.policy: Instructors are encouraged to address in the syllabus the perceived difference between "AI constructing answers" and "using internet resources to learn."

units.why: The definition "(i.e. ChatGPT GPT, DALL-E, Stable Diffusion, Midjourney, GitHub Copilot, and similar tools)" sets which tools the default covers, P61.
units.anchor: (i.e. ChatGPT GPT, DALL-E, Stable Diffusion, Midjourney, GitHub Copilot, and similar tools)
units.policy: The default guidelines cover generative AI tools and foundation models, i.e. ChatGPT GPT, DALL-E, Stable Diffusion, Midjourney, GitHub Copilot, and similar tools.
units.fit_note: Names a code assistant but says nothing about rules for embedded editor tools.

units.why: The default text says AI "is permitted with the following activities in accordance with the stated guidelines at no penalty", a default permission for listed uses. P02 over P107, since the list is permission not a closure of tasks.
units.anchor: is permitted with the following activities in accordance with the stated guidelines at no penalty
units.policy: In courses whose syllabus is unclear, generative AI tools and foundation models (ChatGPT, DALL-E, Stable Diffusion, Midjourney, GitHub Copilot and similar) are permitted for the listed activities at no penalty, in accordance with the stated guidelines.
units.fit_note: Permission is limited to listed activities, with other uses barred below. Permission limited to a listed set of activities (P107-like).

units.why: "Brainstorming and refining your ideas" is a listed permitted use, P15.
units.anchor: Brainstorming and refining your ideas
units.policy: Brainstorming and refining your ideas is permitted with generative AI tools under the default guidelines.

units.why: "Fine tuning your research questions" is a listed permitted use; it is exploring and refining approaches, P15.
units.anchor: Fine tuning your research questions
units.policy: Fine tuning your research questions is permitted with generative AI tools under the default guidelines.

units.why: "Finding information on your topic" is a listed permitted use. P104 (finding sources) is nearest, though it does not mention verifying them.
units.anchor: Finding information on your topic
units.policy: Finding information on your topic is permitted with generative AI tools under the default guidelines.
units.fit_note: Finding information generally, with no condition to read and verify sources.

units.why: "Drafting an outline to organize your thoughts" is a listed permitted use, writing support, P91.
units.anchor: Drafting an outline to organize your thoughts
units.policy: Drafting an outline to organize your thoughts is permitted with generative AI tools under the default guidelines.

units.why: "Checking grammar and style" is a listed permitted use, P91.
units.anchor: Checking grammar and style
units.policy: Checking grammar and style is permitted with generative AI tools under the default guidelines.

units.why: Students must acknowledge "that large language models tend to produce incorrect facts and fake citations." Students are told to expect errors, P31.
units.anchor: large language models tend to produce incorrect facts and fake citations
units.policy: Students are responsible for acknowledging that large language models tend to produce incorrect facts and fake citations.

units.why: "code generation models may produce inaccurate outputs" is a warning on AI code, P31.
units.anchor: code generation models may produce inaccurate outputs
units.policy: Students are responsible for acknowledging that code generation models may produce inaccurate outputs.

units.why: "image generation models can occasionally come up with highly offensive products" names a harm of AI output, P53.
units.anchor: image generation models can occasionally come up with highly offensive products
units.policy: Students are responsible for acknowledging that image generation models can occasionally come up with highly offensive products.

units.why: "Taking responsibility for any inaccurate, biased, offensive, or otherwise unethical content submitted, regardless of the origin". Students own submissions whatever the source, P29.
units.anchor: Taking responsibility for any inaccurate, biased, offensive, or otherwise unethical content submitted
units.policy: Students are responsible for any inaccurate, biased, offensive or otherwise unethical content they submit, whether student-generated or from a foundation model.

units.why: "Properly citing the contribution of the foundation model or other AI tools in submitted material" is a duty to cite AI use, P24.
units.anchor: Properly citing the contribution of the foundation model or other AI tools in submitted material.

units.why: "The entirety of any information they submit, based on an AI query or AI assistance." Students own everything they submit, P29.
units.anchor: The entirety of any information they submit, based on an AI query or AI assistance.

units.why: AI is NOT permitted for "Impersonating students in classroom contexts, such as by using the tool to compose discussion board prompts". P58 (write your own course communication) is nearest; it also names impersonation.
units.anchor: Impersonating students in classroom contexts, such as by using the tool to compose discussion board
units.policy: Generative AI tools are not permitted for impersonating students in classroom contexts, such as composing discussion board prompts or content entered into a Zoom chat.
units.fit_note: Framed as impersonation; covers discussion boards and chat, not only messages to staff. Framed as impersonation in class contexts; P58 is about messages to course staff.

units.why: AI is not permitted for "Completing group work assigned to a student, unless it is mutually agreed upon that they may utilize the tool." A group-work rule, P127.
units.anchor: Completing group work assigned to a student, unless it is mutually agreed upon
units.policy: Generative AI tools are not permitted for completing group work assigned to a student, unless it is mutually agreed upon that they may utilize the tool.

units.why: AI is not permitted for "Writing a draft of a writing assignment." Not to produce submitted text, P19.
units.anchor: Writing a draft of a writing assignment.

units.why: AI is not permitted for "Writing entire sentences, paragraphs or papers to complete class assignments." P19.
units.anchor: Writing entire sentences, paragraphs or papers to complete class assignments.

units.anchor: Using a foundation model without including an acknowledgement.

units.why: Students may be penalized for "Improperly citing the use of work by other human beings or the submission of work by other human beings as that of the student." Misconduct rule about human sources, P36.
units.anchor: Improperly citing the use of work by other human beings
units.policy: Students may be penalized for improperly citing the use of work by other human beings or submitting work by other human beings as their own.
units.fit_note: About work by other humans, not AI. About work of other humans, not AI.

units.why: Students may be penalized for "Violating intellectual property laws." P52.
units.anchor: Violating intellectual property laws.
units.fit_note: States a penalty for IP violations, not guidance on AI outputs. Lists IP violation as a penalizable act without detail.

units.why: Students may be penalized for "Submitting materials containing misinformation or unethical content." Rule against submitting misinformation, P74.
units.anchor: Submitting materials containing misinformation or unethical content.
units.fit_note: Penalizes submitting misinformation, not only deceptive use of AI.

units.why: "The usage of AI tools must be properly cited to stay within university policies on academic honesty." Citation required, P24.

units.policy: Failure to adhere to these guidelines will result in a failing grade on the assignment or exam (a zero).

units.why: "may be an honor code violation depending on the context (to be determined at the instructor's discretion)". Misuse can be handled as misconduct, P36.
units.anchor: may be an honor code violation depending on the context

units.why: "the use of foundation models is encouraged, as it may make it possible for you to submit assignments with higher quality, in less time." An explicit encouragement, P02, which sits uneasily with the listed bans above.
units.anchor: the use of foundation models is encouraged
units.policy: The use of foundation models is encouraged, as it may make it possible to submit assignments with higher quality, in less time.
units.fit_note: Also states a benefit (higher quality, less time), which is P87.

units.anchor: This site provides a sampling of class policies on the use of AI
units.policy: The policy links to a site giving a sampling of class policies on the use of AI.

notes: Coded the three included documents (Provost FAQ, CTE syllabus-statement collection, Data Science policy). Course layer was deferred and the Honor Committee page was inaccessible (Cloudflare), so it was not coded. Within the Data Science policy the ban on drafting writing and the encouragement of foundation models conflict; both were coded as stated. The syllabus-statement collection holds non-computing course examples (English, nursing, law, business, engineering and society) and Provost excerpts; they were coded as the CTE's published examples. Reconciled with coder B (no new types proposed by either coder). The Honor Committee page was inaccessible (Cloudflare) and the course layer was deferred. Dropped units are listed in v2/run/agreement_virginia.json notes.
